# Managed Retreat

The salt came first, as it always did: a grey bloom on the chrome collar of the quarter-inch jack, fine as frost on a fence wire. Nadia worked it loose with her thumbnail before she let herself touch anything else. She kept a toothbrush in the pencil drawer for the rest of it — the card slots, the pins, the little gold teeth of the hub. Salt got into everything. Salt had opinions about the future.

The archive occupied the second floor of the Killick library, which had been a house once and would be a shoal eventually. Up here the sills were still above the spray. Downstairs, what was left of the town's furniture stood in labeled rows waiting for trucks; the state called this a managed retreat, which was the phrase the state used for anything it could not stop. Nadia's job was narrower. On Tuesdays and Thursdays the people of Killick came up the stair and sat in the chair beside the microphone and recorded messages they did not intend to send. Eleven hundred hours of it so far. The grant called the work intangible heritage preservation. Nadia, privately, called it Mr. Pell's fourteenth attempt to explain a Tupperware lid to his brother.

Then the queue coughed up a file it should not have had.

Metadata first, because metadata was the only part of the job that was honest. Duration 4:11. Source: local. Date recorded: a Tuesday in March, ten years ahead. Her initials in the operator field, typed the way she typed them, period and no space.

She played it.

"It's me," her own voice said, and it was hers and it was not — hers the way a photograph is, taken from a distance she had never agreed to. Thinner at the edges. Behind it, a small flat hum she could not place.

"The Ardens' house goes on the second March tide. Not the first. You'll want to be there. Don't go down to the water." A pause, tape-ish, although there was no tape. "Don't rescue the Rickenbacker. You'll want to. Let it go. Say yes to the woman with the ferry." Then: "Record forty minutes of nothing. I'd give anything for forty minutes of nothing." And then the smallest thing, nearly lost: "It was worth it. Even the end part."

Nadia sat with her hands flat on the desk until the dehumidifier clicked and clicked off.

She did what anyone does. She made a list. At first reading the message was a manual written backwards, instructions from somebody who had already failed: don't go, let go, say yes. She underlined *Don't go down to the water* twice, and she noticed the contradiction — you'll want to be there, don't go — and decided that was grief talking, and let it stand.

Everyone in town assumed the February storm would finish the house on Pike, since February had taken its steps and half its dune. February did not finish it. The second tide in March did, at four in the afternoon, in eleven minutes, with a sound like a zipper.

After that, Nadia believed. She believed the way you believe a diagnosis. She stopped walking the shore after work. She let the Rickenbacker — the Ardens' boy's guitar, in its case on the porch, which was to say under the porch — she let it stay. And when Tess, who ran the little ferry out to the survey markers and who had been asking Nadia to come out on the water some Sunday for the better part of a year, asked again at the mailboxes, Nadia heard herself say, "I've got work," and heard, underneath it, the real reason: she would not be moved toward a woman by a voice in a file. She would not be a woman who obeyed.

Tess said *sure* in the particular way she said it. Nadia went upstairs and sat with her hands flat on the desk again.

The file degraded. Everything in the archive degraded; the salt came up through the floor and went looking for current. By April the flat hum behind her own voice had thickened to a hiss, and the line she most needed had gone soft at both ends, so that *Don't go down to the water* arrived as *Don't go — to the water*, with one word in the middle the salt had eaten.

She took the deck apart on a Thursday with nobody scheduled. Boards, ribbon cable, and across the head a film of white like a breath held too long. She brushed it, gently, the way you would brush a child's hair, and set the file to play.

"The Ardens' house goes on the second March tide. Not the first. You'll want to be there. Don't go down to the water without the recorder."

Oh, she thought. Oh.

She played it twice more, and the whole thing turned over in her hands like a stone with a second side.

Not a warning. A commission. The future had not sent back a way to survive. It had sent back a list of what it could no longer have, in the only order a person in a hurry would think to say it: the date, the sound, the one thing worth carrying. Don't go down without the recorder. Let the guitar go — you'll want to, and you'll be sorry, and it's all right. Say yes. This was not a woman escaped from a drowning town calling back to a woman about to drown in it. It was a woman on some inland street with no water in it at all, ten years gone, who wanted forty minutes of a room with west windows and a dehumidifier clicking every eleven minutes, and the only person living who could get it for her was the one person who had never left.

"It was worth it," her older voice said, nearly lost. "Even the end part."

Nadia put the deck back together. She checked the level on the handheld, stretched a fresh foam windscreen over the microphone, and took the stairs two at a time, past the labeled furniture, out into the long flat light. At the landing Tess was idling, engine knocking over, and Nadia held the recorder up so Tess could see it, and Tess, whose *sure* had worn thin as a coin, said it once more, and this time Nadia said, "Yes."

"Sure," said Nadia. "But I'm working."

The house on Pike was gone. The water came in and did its small arithmetic on the stones. Nadia sat on the thwart with the handheld balanced on her knee and recorded the engine, the gulls, the slap under the hull, Tess saying something she could not make out and did not want to. She watched the needle. She gave the future forty minutes of nothing at all, and on the grey foam of the windscreen, slowly, in the air coming off the water, the salt began again.

# Managed Retreat

The salt came first, as always: a grey bloom on the chrome collar of the quarter-inch jack, fine as frost on a fence wire. Nadia worked it loose with her thumbnail before she let herself touch anything else. She kept a toothbrush in the pencil drawer for the rest of it — the card slots, the pins, the little gold teeth of the hub. Salt got everywhere. Salt had opinions about the future.

The archive occupied the second floor of the Killick library, which had been a house once and would be a shoal eventually. Up here the sills were still above the spray. Downstairs, the town's remaining furniture stood in labeled rows, waiting for the trucks; the state called this a managed retreat, which was the phrase the state used for everything it could not stop. Nadia's job was narrower. On Tuesdays and Thursdays the people of Killick came up the stair and sat in the chair beside the microphone and recorded messages they did not intend to send. Eleven hundred hours of it so far. The grant called the work intangible heritage preservation; Nadia, privately, called it Mr. Pell's fourteenth attempt to explain a Tupperware lid to his brother.

Then the queue coughed up a file it shouldn't have had.

Metadata first, because metadata was the only part of the job that was honest. Duration 4:11. Source: local. Date recorded: a Tuesday in March, ten years ahead. Her own initials in the operator field, N.R., typed the way she typed them, with the period and no space.

She played it.

"It's me," her own voice said, and it was hers and it wasn't — hers the way a photograph is, taken from a distance she hadn't agreed to. Older. Thinner at the edges. Behind it, a small flat hum she couldn't place.

"The Ardens' house goes on the second March tide," the voice said. "Not the first. You'll want to be there. Don't go down to the water." A pause, tape-ish, although there was no tape. "Don't rescue the Rickenbacker. You'll want to. Let it go. Say yes to the woman with the ferry." Then: "Record forty minutes of nothing. I'd give anything for forty minutes of nothing." And then the smallest thing, nearly lost: "It was worth it. Even the end part."

Nadia sat with her hands flat on the desk until the dehumidifier clicked and clicked off.

She did what anyone would do. She made a list. The message read, at first, like a survival manual written backward: a set of instructions from someone who had already failed. Don't go. Let go. Say yes. She underlined "Don't go down to the water" twice. The Ardens' house was the last one on Pike Street, out on the point, and the February storm had already taken its porch steps and half its dune; everyone in town assumed February would finish it. February did not finish it. The second tide in March did, at four in the afternoon, in eleven minutes, with a sound like a zipper.

After that, Nadia believed.

She believed in the way you believe a diagnosis. She stopped walking the shore after work. She let the Rickenbacker — the Ardens' boy's guitar, still in its case on the porch, which is to say under the porch — she let it stay. And when Tess, who ran the little ferry out to the survey markers and who had been asking Nadia to come out on the water with her on a Sunday for most of a year, asked again at the mailboxes on a gray morning, Nadia heard herself say, "I've got work," and heard, underneath it, the reason: she would not be moved by a voice in a file toward a woman she had not chosen for herself. She would not be a woman who obeyed.

Tess said, "Sure," in the particular way she said it, and Nadia went upstairs and sat with her hands flat on the desk again.

The file degraded. It did that; everything in the archive did. The salt came up through the floor and went looking for current. By April the small flat hum behind her own voice had thickened into a hiss, and the line she most needed had gone soft at the edges, so that "Don't go down to the water" arrived as "Don't go — to the water," with something swallowed in the middle, a word the salt had eaten.

She took the deck apart on a Thursday with no one scheduled. Boards, ribbon, a film of white across the head like a breath held too long. She brushed it. She did it gently, the way you'd brush a child's hair, and set the file to play.

"The Ardens' house goes on the second March tide. Not the first. You'll want to be there. Don't go down to the water without the recorder."

Oh, she thought. Oh.

She played it again, and then the whole thing turned over in her hands like something with a second side.

Not a warning. A commission. The future hadn't sent back instructions for surviving; it had sent back a list of the things it could no longer have, in the only order a person in a panic would think to say them: the date, the sound, the one thing to carry. Don't go down without the recorder. Let the guitar go, you'll want to. Say yes. It was not a woman escaping a drowning town speaking to a woman about to drown in it. It was a woman on a shoreless inland street somewhere, ten years gone, who wanted forty minutes of a room with west windows, and the only person alive who could get it for her was the one person who had never left.

"It was worth it," her older voice said, nearly lost, "even the end part."

Nadia put the deck back together. She checked the level on the handheld, wound a fresh windscreen over the microphone — grey foam, already gritted — and took the stairs two at a time, out past the labeled furniture, out into the long flat light. At the landing Tess was idling, engine knocking over, and Nadia held up the recorder so Tess could see it, and Tess, who had said "sure" so many times that the word had worn thin, said it again, and this time Nadia said, "Yes."

Then: "But I'm working."

The house on Pike was gone. The water came in and did its small arithmetic on the stones. Nadia sat on the thwart with the handheld balanced on her knee and recorded the engine, the gulls, the slap under the hull, Tess saying something she couldn't make out and didn't want to. She watched the level. She gave the future forty minutes of nothing at all, and on the foam of the windscreen, slowly, in the air off the water, the salt began again.

Everyone assumed the February storm would finish the house on Pike, since February had taken its steps and half its dune. February did not finish it. The second tide in March did, at four in the afternoon, in eleven minutes, with a sound like a zipper.

After that, Nadia believed, the way you believe a diagnosis. She stopped walking the shore after work. She let the Rickenbacker — the Ardens' boy's guitar, in its case on the porch, which was to say under the porch — she let it stay. And when Tess, who ran the ferry out to the survey markers and had been asking Nadia out on the water for the better part of a year, asked again at the mailboxes, Nadia heard herself say, "I've got work," and heard, underneath it, the real reason: she would not be moved toward a woman by a voice in a file.

Tess said *sure* in the particular way she said it. Nadia went upstairs and sat with her hands flat on the desk again.
